title: Assignment, exercise and expiry
teaches: How exercise and assignment work, what happens at the bell on expiry day, when early assignment comes, and the words for how a position ends: closed, expired, exercised, assigned or rolled.

sources.publisher: The Options Clearing Corporation and the US options exchanges
sources.title: Characteristics and Risks of Standardized Options (June 2024 edition)
sources.why_reliable: The official options disclosure document every options customer must receive (June 2024 edition, which carries the T+1 exercise settlement amendment; no later edition was found on 2026-11-09). theocc.com refuses plain clients (403, checked 2026-11-09), so this cites the copy Robinhood distributes to its customers (cover: June 2024; copyright the exchanges and OCC).

sources.title: What Is Dividend Risk? Basics and Examples
Equity Options Extended Trading Hours FAQ (last updated November 2, 2026)

facts.quote: They first must direct their brokerage firm to submit an exercise notice to OCC.
facts.claim: To exercise, the holder tells their broker, and the broker sends an exercise notice to OCC.

facts.quote: OCC then randomly assigns the exercise notice to a clearing member. For an investor, this is generally his brokerage firm chosen at random from a total pool of such firms.
facts.claim: OCC assigns each exercise at random to a clearing firm, usually a brokerage.

facts.quote: Assignment to a customer is either random or on a first-in-first-out basis. This depends on the firm’s method.
facts.claim: Your broker picks which short customer is assigned at random or first in, first out, by its own method.

facts.quote: If an option writer is short an option that expires in-the-money, they should expect assignment on that contract, though assignment is not guaranteed as some long in-the-money option holders may elect not to exercise in-the-money options.
facts.claim: Short an option that expires in the money, expect assignment, though it isn't guaranteed.

facts.quote: In fact, some option writers are assigned on short contracts when they expire exactly at-the-money or even out-of-the money. This occurrence is usually not predictable.
facts.claim: Writers are sometimes assigned on options that expire at the money or even out of the money.

facts.quote: To avoid assignment on a written option contract on a given day, the position must be closed out before that day's market close.
facts.claim: The only way to avoid assignment on a given day is to close the short before that day's close.

facts.quote: Although this is not always the case as post-market underlying moves may lead to out-of-the-money options being exercised and in-the-money options not being exercised.
facts.claim: After-hours moves can get out-of-the-money options exercised and in-the-money ones left unexercised.

facts.quote: is assigned an exercise notice on that put, the net price paid for the underlying stock on per share basis is the sum of the put's strike price less the premium received
facts.claim: An assigned put writer's net cost per share is the strike minus the premium they collected.

facts.quote: Investors should expect this as expiration nears with a call considerably in-the-money and a sizeable dividend payment approaching. Call writers should be aware of dividend dates and the possibility of early assignment.
facts.claim: Expect early assignment on a short call that is well in the money with a sizeable dividend coming.

facts.quote: When puts become deep in-the-money, most professional option traders exercise before expiration.
facts.claim: Deep in-the-money puts are usually exercised before expiry by professionals.

facts.quote: OCC uses the $.01 threshold for the positions of its clearing members as an administrative convenience, but your firm may have a different threshold.
facts.claim: OCC's automatic-exercise threshold is one cent in the money; your broker may use a different one.

facts.quote: The option holder can always submit instructions to their broker regarding whether to exercise or not to exercise.
facts.claim: A holder can always tell the broker to exercise or not to exercise.

facts.quote: Historically, more than 72% of all option contracts are closed out in the market prior to expiration. Additionally, another 22% expire without value while the remaining 6% get exercised.
facts.claim: Historically most option contracts are closed before expiry; about one in five expire worthless and only a few percent are exercised.

facts.quote: The exercise style of an option does not prevent an investor from closing the position via a transaction on an exchange any time up to and including the last trading day.
facts.claim: Exercise style doesn't stop you closing the position on any trading day up to the last one.

facts.quote: An option holder can only exercise a European-style exercise option at expiration, so the only way to close your position prior to expiration is to execute a closing trade.
facts.claim: A European-style option can only be exercised at expiry; before that you close it with a trade.

facts.quote: A call holder is entitled to the dividend if the holder exercises the call prior to the ex-dividend date. An assigned call writer (covered or not) is obligated to deliver the stock plus the dividend.
facts.claim: A holder who exercises before the ex-date gets the dividend, and the assigned call writer owes the stock plus the dividend.

facts.quote: The difference between the exercise price and the “closing price” of the underlying security determine whether expiring options are in-the-money or not.
facts.claim: Whether an expiring option counts as in the money is set by the stock's closing price.

facts.quote: When an option holder exercises an option early, they forfeit any time value priced into the option. This is one reason that an option holder might not exercise an option early.
facts.claim: Exercising early throws away the option's time value, one reason a holder might not.

facts.quote: As the ex-date for a dividend approaches, there is increased likelihood that call holders will exercise in-the-money calls.
facts.claim: In-the-money calls are more likely to be exercised as an ex-dividend date nears.

facts.quote: Options exchanges have a cut-off time of 4:30 p.m. CT, for receiving an exercise notice. Be aware that most brokerage firms have an earlier cut-off time for submitting exercise instructions
facts.claim: The exchanges' exercise cut-off is 4:30 p.m. Central (5:30 p.m. Eastern), and most brokers set an earlier one.

facts.quote: If a physical delivery put option is exercised, the assigned writer must purchase the required number of shares at the specified exercise price regardless of their current market price.
facts.claim: An assigned put writer must buy the shares at the strike, whatever the market price.

facts.quote: Assignments are ordinarily made prior to the commencement of trading on the business day following receipt by OCC of the exercise instruction.
facts.claim: OCC ordinarily assigns an exercise before trading opens on the next business day.

facts.quote: It is possible that an option writer will not receive notification from its brokerage firm that an exercise has been assigned to him until one or more days following the date of the initial assignment
facts.claim: A writer may not hear about an assignment until a day or more after OCC made it.

facts.quote: Once an exercise has been assigned to a writer, the writer may no longer close out the assigned position in a closing purchase transaction, whether or not she has received notice of the assignment.
facts.claim: After assignment, the writer can't close that short by buying it back, even before the notice arrives.

facts.quote: In that circumstance, an attempted closing purchase would be treated as an opening purchase transaction.
facts.claim: A buy-back after assignment just opens a new long option.

facts.quote: As of May 28, 2024, the regular exercise settlement date for physical delivery stock options is the first business day after exercise.
facts.claim: Since May 28, 2024, exercised stock options settle on the first business day after exercise.

facts.quote: Cash-settled index options whose exercise settlement values are based on the opening prices of the constituent securities are not traded on the option expiration date
facts.claim: Index options settled on opening prices (AM-settled) don't trade on their expiration date.

facts.quote: An option that expires unexercised becomes worthless.
facts.claim: An option that expires without being exercised is worth nothing.

facts.quote: An option holder looks to the system created by OCC’s rules, rather than to any particular option writer, for performance of the option he owns.
facts.claim: A holder deals with OCC's system, not with the particular person who sold the option.

facts.quote: an investor must keep in mind the possibility of being assigned an exercise, which would eliminate that component of the transaction and could materially change the investor’s risk position.
facts.claim: Assignment on one leg of a combination removes that leg and can change your risk a lot.

facts.quote: there is a risk that an option writer will be assigned an exercise that is made based on news that is published after the established exercise cut-off time
facts.claim: A writer can even be assigned on an exercise based on news published after the cut-off.

facts.quote: This Rule provides that, unless contrary instructions are given, standardized equity option contracts that are in-the-money by specified amounts shall be automatically exercised.
facts.claim: Under OCC's exercise-by-exception rule, expiring equity options in the money by set amounts are exercised unless told otherwise.

facts.quote: Exercise cut-off time. Option holders have until 5:30 p.m. Eastern Time ("ET") on the business day of expiration
facts.claim: Under FINRA's rule, holders have until 5:30 p.m. ET on expiry day to make the final exercise decision.

facts.quote: Members may establish a processing cut-off time prior to FINRA's exercise cut-off time at which they will no longer accept final exercise decisions in expiring standardized equity options from customers.
facts.claim: Your broker may set an earlier cut-off than FINRA's.

facts.quote: Members may not accept exercise instructions for customer or non-customer accounts after 5:30 p.m. ET.
facts.claim: Brokers can't accept exercise instructions after 5:30 p.m. ET.

facts.quote: Such allocation shall be on a "first in-first out" or automated random selection basis that has been approved by FINRA or on a manual random selection basis that has been specified by FINRA.
facts.claim: Brokers must allocate assignments first in, first out or by random selection.

facts.quote: (1) not exercise an option position which would automatically be exercised pursuant to The Options Clearing Corporation's Ex-by-Ex procedure; or (2) to exercise a standardized equity option position which would not automatically be exercised
facts.claim: A contrary instruction can stop an automatic exercise, or exercise an option that wouldn't be exercised automatically.

facts.quote: The exercise cut-off requirements contained in this subparagraph (A) do not apply to any currency option or standardized index option products listed on a national options exchange.
facts.claim: The 5:30 p.m. ET cut-off rule covers stock and ETF options, not index options.

facts.quote: the deadline for an option holder to make a final decision to exercise or not exercise an expiring option shall be 1 hour 30 minutes following the time announced for the close of trading on that day
facts.claim: On an early-close day, the exercise deadline is an hour and a half after the announced close.

facts.quote: the Options Clearing Corporation (OCC), which is the options industry clearing house, has an established process to randomly assign exercise notices to firms with an account that has a short option position.
facts.claim: OCC assigns exercise notices at random to firms that carry short positions in that option.

facts.quote: Only about 7% of options positions are typically exercised, but that does not imply that investors can expect to be assigned on only 7% of their short positions.
facts.claim: Only about 7% of option positions are exercised, but that says nothing about your own short being safe.

facts.quote: An option assignment represents the seller's obligation to fulfill the terms of the contract by either selling or buying the underlying security at the exercise price.
facts.claim: Assignment is the seller's obligation to sell or buy the shares at the strike.

facts.quote: If the investor owns an option that serves to limit the risk of the overall spread position, it is up to the investor to exercise that option or to take other action to limit risk.
facts.claim: When a spread's short leg is assigned, exercising or managing the long leg is up to you.

facts.quote: However, due to an unexpected news announcement shortly after the closing bell, the price of XYZ drops to $40 in after-hours trading. This could result in an assignment of the short March 50 puts
facts.claim: In FINRA's example, after-hours news drops the stock to 40 and the out-of-the-money short 50 puts can be assigned.

facts.quote: The investor would have needed to exercise the long March 55 puts in order to realize the gain on the initial multi-leg position.
facts.claim: In that example, the trader has to exercise the long 55 puts to get the spread's gain.

facts.quote: If the investor did not exercise the March 55 puts, those puts may expire and the investor may be exposed to the loss on the XYZ purchase at $50
facts.claim: If the long 55 puts aren't exercised, they expire and the trader carries the loss on shares bought at 50.

facts.quote: as long as a short options position remains open, the seller may be subject to "assignment" on any day equity markets are open.
facts.claim: An open short American-style option can be assigned on any trading day.

facts.quote: A trading action in which the trader simultaneously closes an open option position and creates a new option position at a different strike price, different expiration, or both.
facts.claim: Rolling means closing an option and opening a new one at a different strike, expiry, or both, at the same time.

facts.quote: The risk to an investor (option writer) that the stock price will exactly equal the strike price at expiration (that option will be exactly at-the-money).
facts.claim: Pin risk is the writer's risk that the stock finishes right at the strike on expiry.

facts.quote: The risk is that on the following Monday the option writer might have an unexpected long (in the case of a written put) or short (in the case of a written call) stock position
facts.claim: With a pinned short, you may find an unexpected stock position on Monday.

facts.quote: Notification by OCC to a clearing member that an owner of an option has exercised their rights. For equity and index options, OCC makes assignments on a random basis.
facts.claim: Assignment is OCC's notice that a holder has exercised; OCC assigns at random.

facts.quote: To invoke the rights granted to the owner of an option contract. In the case of a call, the option owner buys the underlying stock. In the case of a put, the option owner sells the underlying stock.
facts.claim: Exercise is the holder using the right: a call buys the stock, a put sells it.

facts.quote: The date that an option and the right to exercise it cease to exist.
facts.claim: At expiration, the option and the right to exercise it stop existing.

facts.quote: Unless instructed not to do so, all expiring equity options held in customer accounts are exercised if they are in-the-money by a specified amount.
facts.claim: Expiring equity options in customer accounts are exercised if in the money by a set amount, unless told not to.

facts.quote: Early assignment, while possible at any time, generally occurs only when a put option goes deep into-the-money.
facts.claim: Early assignment on a short put generally comes only once it is deep in the money.

facts.quote: Be warned, however, that using the long put to cover the short put assignment will require financing a long stock position for one business day.
facts.claim: Covering an assigned short put with your long put still means carrying the shares for a business day.

facts.quote: The investor cannot know for sure whether or not they will be assigned on the short put until the Monday after expiration.
facts.claim: Near the strike, you won't know about a short put's assignment until the Monday after expiry.

facts.quote: Early assignment, while possible at any time, generally occurs when the stock goes ex-dividend.
facts.claim: Early assignment on a short call generally comes around the ex-dividend date.

facts.quote: the short call ends up slightly in-the-money, and the investor buys the stock in the market in anticipation of being assigned. If assignment fails to occur, the investor won't discover the unintended net long stock position until the following Monday
facts.claim: Buying stock in advance of an expected assignment can leave you unexpectedly long on Monday if the assignment never comes.

facts.quote: Two ways to prepare: close the spread out early, or be prepared for either outcome on Monday.
facts.claim: Near the strike at expiry, either close the position early or be ready for either outcome Monday.

facts.quote: The problem is most acute if the stock is trading just below, at or just above the short call strike.
facts.claim: The not-knowing is worst when the stock sits right around the short strike.

facts.quote: Unfortunately, in general it is not optimal to exercise a call option until the last day before expiration. An exception to that general rule occurs the day before a stock goes ex-dividend
facts.claim: Exercising a call early usually doesn't pay, except the day before the stock goes ex-dividend.

facts.quote: The investor must be comfortable with the strike price as an acceptable long-term acquisition price, no matter how low the market goes.
facts.claim: Only sell a put at a strike you'd accept as your price for the shares, however low the stock goes.

facts.quote: Trading in SPX options will ordinarily cease on the business day (usually a Thursday) preceding the day on which the exercise-settlement value (i.e., the expiration date) is calculated
facts.claim: Standard AM-settled SPX options stop trading the business day before expiry, usually a Thursday.

facts.quote: Trading in SPXW options will ordinarily cease on the day of expiration, 4:00 pm ET
facts.claim: PM-settled SPXW options trade until 4:00 p.m. ET on expiry day.

facts.quote: Options can only be exercised at expiration, providing certainty and eliminating early assignment risk.
facts.claim: European-style SPX options can only be exercised at expiry, so there's no early assignment.

facts.quote: Positions settle directly to cash at expiration without the need to deliver or receive unwanted shares
facts.claim: SPX options settle in cash, with no shares delivered.

facts.quote: On expiration day, options are typically automatically exercised if they're ITM by $0.01 or more as of 3 p.m. CT. In general, the option holder has until 4:30 p.m. CT on expiration day to exercise the contract.
facts.claim: Options in the money by $0.01 or more at the close are typically exercised automatically; holders can decide until 4:30 p.m. Central.

facts.quote: However, if the price of the underlying security changes after the close, a trader might have a short option go from OTM to ITM. The option holder may choose to exercise
facts.claim: An after-hours move can turn a short option from out of the money to in the money, and the holder may exercise.

facts.quote: If the 90-strike call is ITM and the 95-strike call is OTM at expiration, the lower-strike call will be subject to automatic exercise and the 95-strike call will likely expire worthless.
facts.claim: In a 90/95 call spread finishing between the strikes, the 90 call is exercised and the 95 call likely expires.

facts.quote: Therefore, a trader would buy the shares for $90 unless they close the position by selling the spread prior to expiration (or submit a DNE for the ITM call).
facts.claim: That leaves you buying shares at 90 unless you sell the spread first or file a do-not-exercise.

facts.quote: Some index options are AM-settled, meaning they're settled Friday morning but typically stop trading Thursday afternoon.
facts.claim: AM-settled index options typically stop trading Thursday and settle Friday morning.

facts.quote: So-called print risk is the overnight risk of AM-settled options.
facts.claim: AM-settled options carry overnight risk between Thursday's close and Friday's settlement.

facts.quote: DNEs—which can be submitted by any option holder—instruct the broker not to auto-exercise ITM options at expiration.
facts.claim: Any holder can file a do-not-exercise to stop an automatic exercise.

facts.quote: On their final trading day, trading in expiring PM-settled options typically ends at 3 p.m. CT, apart from some broad-based exchange-traded fund (ETF) options, which trade until 3:15 p.m. CT.
facts.claim: Expiring PM-settled options typically stop trading at the 3 p.m. Central close, some ETF options a little later.

facts.quote: If a trader is unsure if they have enough cash or margin, or if they don't want the position, it's generally better to liquidate the option before market close.
facts.claim: If you don't want the shares, sell the option before the close.

facts.quote: Also, standard equity options are not cash-settled—actual shares are transferred during exercise/assignment.
facts.claim: Stock options settle in shares, not cash.

facts.quote: An option seller might be more likely to get assigned on a short call prior to an upcoming ex-dividend date if its time value is less than the dividend.
facts.claim: A short call is more likely to be assigned before an ex-date when its time value is less than the dividend.

facts.quote: It's more likely to get assigned holding a short put if the time value has mostly decayed or if the put is deep ITM and close to expiration with a wide bid/ask spread on the stock.
facts.claim: A short put is more likely to be assigned when its time value is mostly gone or it is deep in the money near expiry.

facts.quote: Essentially, any long call option that has extrinsic value of less than the dividend amount (minus fees and transaction costs) might be a candidate for early exercise.
facts.claim: A call whose time value is below the dividend is a candidate for early exercise.

facts.quote: This early assignment forces the option seller to deliver the underlying shares at the strike price and effectively pay the dividend amount to the buyer.
facts.claim: Assigned before the ex-date, the call seller delivers shares at the strike and effectively pays the dividend.

facts.quote: a trader might consider avoiding early assignment ahead of a dividend by either buying back the call option or rolling it to another option, such as a higher strike call or a call with a later expiration date
facts.claim: To avoid dividend assignment, buy the call back or roll it to a higher strike or later expiry.

facts.quote: If a covered call option you have sold is in the money and the dividend exceeds the remaining time value of the option, there is a good chance an owner of those calls will exercise his options early.
facts.claim: When the dividend exceeds a short call's remaining time value, early exercise is likely.

facts.quote: Because the remaining time value of the call option is less than the value of the dividends, the call owner will likely exercise his options on the day before the ex-dividend date.
facts.claim: Those calls are likely exercised on the day before the ex-dividend date.

facts.quote: If his calls are assigned, however, he will have to pay the $250 in dividend income, in addition to covering the cost of delivering 500 shares of ABC stock.
facts.claim: An assigned uncovered call writer pays the dividend on every share delivered: $250 on 500 shares in Fidelity's example.

facts.quote: If both contracts are in the money and you are assigned on the short contracts, you will not be notified until the following business day.
facts.claim: You learn of an assignment the following business day.

facts.quote: The other option is to close out his short position and write a new covered call with a later expiration date or a higher strike price. This strategy is known as "rolling" your options contract forward.
facts.claim: Closing a short call and selling a new one further out or higher up is called rolling.

facts.quote: Expiring equity single stock options will trade until 4:00 p.m. ET as part of RTH and 4:15 p.m. ET in the Curb session on expiration day
facts.claim: In the select stocks Cboe opens to extended hours, expiring options can trade until 4:15 p.m. ET on expiry day.

facts.quote: OCC also bases in/out-of-the-money determination based on the 4:00 p.m. ET closing price of the underlying equity security.
facts.claim: OCC decides whether an expiring stock option is in the money from the stock's 4:00 p.m. ET close.

walkthroughs.title: Who gets the notice
steps: To exercise, the holder tells their broker, and the broker sends the notice to the Options Clearing Corporation (OCC).
OCC hands it at random to a broker that carries shorts in that option.
That broker picks one of its short customers, at random or first in, first out.
That writer is assigned and must buy or sell the shares at the strike, whatever the market price.

walkthroughs.title: The bell on expiry day
steps: On expiry day, a stock option a cent ($0.01) or more in the money at the close is usually exercised.
Holders can say no, and FINRA's rule gives them until 5:30 p.m. ET to decide. After-hours news can still flip it.
Writers usually hear the next business day. On a Friday expiry, that means Monday.

walkthroughs.title: When early assignment comes
steps: Stock options are American-style, so a short can be assigned on any trading day.
A short call is most at risk the day before an ex-dividend date, when its time value is below the dividend.
A short put is most at risk once it's deep in the money.
European-style index options like SPX can only be exercised at expiry, so they carry no early assignment.

questions.q: In options, what does assignment mean?
choices: The seller must now fulfill the contract
The buyer uses the right to buy or sell
Closing it and opening a new strike
questions.answer: The seller must now fulfill the contract
questions.why: The seller must now fulfill the contract. A holder exercised, OCC passed the notice on, and the writer must buy or sell the shares at the strike.
questions.lesson_line: Exercise is the buyer's move. Assignment is what lands on the seller.

wrong.The buyer uses the right to buy or sell: That's exercise, the holder's side. Assignment is what an exercise triggers for a writer.
wrong.The option ran out worthless: That's an option that expired. Once it expires, it and the right to exercise it are gone.
wrong.Closing it and opening a new strike: That's rolling: closing one option and opening another at a new strike or expiry.

questions.q: Most option contracts end by being exercised.
questions.why: False. Historically, the Options Industry Council counts more than 72% of contracts closed out before expiry, 22% expiring worthless and only 6% exercised. FINRA puts exercises at about 7%.
questions.lesson_line: Most options are sold or bought back before expiry. Exercise is the exception.

questions.q: Many traders are short the same call. A holder exercises one. How is the writer who must deliver chosen?
choices: OCC at random, then your broker's method
The holder picks who sold to them
questions.answer: OCC at random, then your broker's method
questions.why: OCC at random, then your broker's method. OCC hands the notice to a clearing broker at random, and that broker picks a short customer at random or first in, first out.
questions.lesson_line: You can't predict who gets assigned. If you're short the option, assume it can be you.

wrong.The holder picks who sold to them: The holder deals with OCC's system, not with the person who sold to them.
wrong.The biggest short goes first: Size doesn't set the order. OCC picks at random, then the broker uses random selection or first in, first out.
wrong.Whoever sold most recently: Under first in, first out the oldest short goes first, not the newest. Other brokers pick at random.

questions.q: You buy back your short May 50 call and sell a June 55 call in one trade. What is that called?
questions.why: Rolling. You close one option and open another at a new strike, a new expiry, or both, at the same time.
questions.lesson_line: A roll is two trades in one: close the old option, open the new one.

wrong.Exercising: Exercising uses an option's right to buy or sell the shares. You traded the options instead.
wrong.Being assigned: Assignment comes to you from OCC. Here you chose to close and reopen.
wrong.Letting it expire: You closed the May call before expiry and opened a new one.

questions.q: Fill in the blank.
questions.sentence: At expiry, OCC exercises an equity option in the money by a ___ or more, unless told not to.
questions.why: A penny. OCC's threshold is $0.01 at the close, and your broker may use its own. You can always tell your broker to exercise or not.
questions.lesson_line: A penny in the money at the close is enough. Plan for exercise unless you say otherwise.

questions.q: You can't sell a European-style option before its expiry day.
questions.why: False. European style limits when you can exercise, not when you can trade. You can close it on any trading day up to the last one.
questions.lesson_line: Exercise style decides when you can exercise. You can sell either style on any trading day up to the last.

questions.q: You're short an in-the-money call on a stock that pays a dividend. When is early assignment most likely?
choices: The first week after you sell it
Any day the stock closes higher
questions.why: Just before the ex-dividend date. A holder who exercises the day before the ex-date collects the dividend. Most other days, exercising early just throws away time value.
questions.lesson_line: If you're short calls on a dividend payer, mark the ex-dividend date. That's when early assignment usually comes.

wrong.The morning after earnings: Earnings alone don't make early exercise pay. It throws away time value, and a coming dividend is the usual reason to do it.
wrong.The first week after you sell it: Early in its life the call carries more time value, and exercising would throw it away.
wrong.Any day the stock closes higher: A higher close alone doesn't pay a holder to exercise. Selling the call keeps its time value.

questions.q: You're short four puts on different stocks. Which one is most likely to be assigned early?
choices: Deep in the money, near expiry
Just in the money, months to go
At the money, expiry this week
Out of the money, ex-date soon
questions.answer: Deep in the money, near expiry
questions.why: Deep in the money, near expiry. Its time value is mostly gone, so a holder gives up almost nothing by exercising early.
questions.lesson_line: A deep in-the-money short put can be assigned any day. Close it, or be ready to buy the shares.

wrong.Just in the money, months to go: With months left it still carries time value, which an early exercise would throw away.
wrong.At the money, expiry this week: At the money there's nothing in the money to collect. Exercising would sell at about the market price.
wrong.Out of the money, ex-date soon: Out of the money, exercising means selling below the market. Ex-dividend dates pull in call holders, not put holders.

questions.q: An exercised stock option settles two business days after the exercise.
questions.why: False. As of May 28, 2024, an exercised stock option settles on the first business day after exercise. Exercise on a Friday, and it normally settles Monday.
questions.lesson_line: Exercise and assignment settle the next business day. Have the cash or the shares ready.

questions.q: Under FINRA's rule as of November 2026, until when can a holder decide to exercise an expiring stock option?
questions.why: 5:30 p.m. ET on expiry day. On an early-close day it moves to an hour and a half after the close, and your broker can set an earlier cut-off.
questions.lesson_line: Expiry day runs past the bell. Holders can still decide until 5:30 p.m. ET.

wrong.4:00 p.m. ET, the closing bell: That's when the stock market closes. Holders still have until 5:30 p.m. ET to decide.
wrong.Midnight ET on expiry day: Firms can't accept exercise instructions after 5:30 p.m. ET.
wrong.9:30 a.m. ET the next morning: By then the option has expired, and an option that expires unexercised is worthless.

questions.q: On Tuesday, a holder exercises a call you're short. When is the exercise usually assigned?
questions.why: Before trading opens Wednesday. OCC ordinarily assigns exercises before the next business day's open, and your broker's notice can come a day or more after that.
questions.lesson_line: Assignment lands overnight. You find out after the fact, sometimes later.

wrong.Instantly, during Tuesday's session: OCC assigns overnight, before the next day's open, not while the market trades.
wrong.Only at the option's expiry: Stock options are American-style. A short can be assigned on any trading day.
wrong.Within a week, after settlement: Assignment comes first, ordinarily before the next open. Settlement follows it.

questions.q: Once you're assigned, buying the option back won't undo it, even if you haven't seen the notice yet.
questions.why: True. Once an exercise is assigned to you, you can't close that short with a purchase, notice or not. The buy just opens a new long option.
questions.lesson_line: Assignment can't be undone. Close a short you don't want before the bell, not after.

questions.q: Short 3 calls, no shares. Exercised the day before the ex-date, and you're assigned. Dividend: $0.40 a share. What dividend do you owe?
questions.why: $120. Assigned on an exercise made before the ex-date, you're short the shares going into it, so you owe the dividend: 3 contracts of 100 shares at $0.40.
questions.lesson_line: Short calls with no shares, assigned before the ex-date, leave you owing the dividend too.

questions.story: You own a 90/95 call spread: long the 90 call, short the 95 call, same expiry. On expiry Friday the stock closes at 93. You do nothing.
questions.q: What are you most likely holding on Monday?
choices: Cash for the spread, no shares
questions.why: 100 shares, bought at 90. The 90 call is in the money at the close, so it's exercised. The 95 call is out of the money and likely expires.
questions.lesson_line: Between the strikes at expiry, a long call spread turns into stock. Sell the spread first if you don't want shares.

wrong.Cash for the spread, no shares: Stock options settle in shares, not cash. The exercised 90 call buys you the shares.
wrong.Short 100 shares at 95: At 93 the 95 call is out of the money, so it most likely expires unexercised.
wrong.Nothing, both legs expire: The 90 call is in the money at the close, so it's exercised unless you say otherwise.

questions.q: A short option that's out of the money at the close on expiry day can still be assigned.
questions.why: True. Holders have until 5:30 p.m. ET to decide, and after-hours news can push an option into the money. Writers are sometimes assigned on options that expired out of the money.
questions.lesson_line: Out of the money at the bell isn't safe yet. If a short sits near the strike, close it or be ready.

questions.story: You're short the 55 call with no shares. The stock is 62.40 and goes ex-dividend tomorrow, paying 0.30. Your call trades at 7.45, two weeks from expiry.
questions.q: How likely is an early assignment tonight?
choices: Likely: just $0.05 of time value left
Unlikely: two weeks are still left
Unlikely: holders wait for expiry day
Unlikely: the dividend is too small
questions.answer: Likely: just $0.05 of time value left
questions.why: Likely. The call has only $0.05 of time value, less than the 0.30 dividend. A holder who exercises today gives up 0.05 to collect 0.30.
questions.lesson_line: When a short call's time value is below the coming dividend, expect assignment. Buy it back or roll it before the ex-date.

wrong.Unlikely: two weeks are still left: Time left doesn't protect you. The time value left is what matters, and here it's tiny.
wrong.Unlikely: holders wait for expiry day: That's the general rule, and the day before an ex-dividend date is the exception.
wrong.Unlikely: the dividend is too small: Small isn't the test. The dividend only has to beat the $0.05 of time value a holder gives up.

questions.story: You sold one 45 put for 1.80. On expiry Friday the stock closes at 43.50. You don't close the put.
questions.q: What do you most likely hold on Monday, and at what net cost?
questions.why: 100 shares, net cost $43.20. You buy at the 45 strike, and the 1.80 you collected brings your cost down. In the money at the close, expect assignment, usually confirmed Monday.
questions.lesson_line: Only sell a put at a strike you'd be happy to pay. Assignment means you pay it.

wrong.100 shares at $43.50, the close: You buy at the 45 strike, not the market price. The 1.80 premium is what lowers your cost.
wrong.Nothing: the put just expires: It's in the money at the close, so it's exercised unless the holder says otherwise.
wrong.Short 100 shares at $45: An assigned short put makes you buy shares. Short shares come from an assigned short call.

questions.story: You sold the 50/45 put spread: short the 50 put, long the 45 put. Two weeks before expiry the stock drops to 41, and your 50 put is assigned.
questions.q: What's in your account now?
choices: Short 100 shares at 50, plus the 45 put
Cash for the max loss, spread closed
questions.why: 100 shares at 50, plus the 45 put. Assignment hits only the short leg. The 45 put is still yours, and it's up to you to exercise it or sell it.
questions.lesson_line: Assignment breaks a spread. The long leg is still yours to exercise or sell, so act on it.

wrong.Nothing, the spread closed itself: The legs aren't tied together. The long put stays open until you act on it or it expires.
wrong.Short 100 shares at 50, plus the 45 put: An assigned short put makes you buy shares, so you're long, not short.
wrong.Cash for the max loss, spread closed: Stock options settle in shares, leg by leg. The spread doesn't settle as one cash amount.

questions.story: It's expiry Friday. You're short one 50 call and own no shares. At 3:50 p.m. ET the stock sits at 50.02.
questions.q: What's the cleanest way to avoid a surprise position on Monday?
choices: Buy the call back before the close
Nothing, two cents won't get exercised
Buy 100 shares in case of assignment
Wait and see the after-hours price
questions.answer: Buy the call back before the close
questions.why: Buy it back before the close. Right at the strike you can't know if you'll be assigned until Monday. Closing the short is the only sure way out.
questions.lesson_line: Right at the strike on expiry day, I close the short. Guessing at assignment is how you get a Monday surprise.

wrong.Nothing, two cents won't get exercised: The automatic threshold is $0.01. If it closes at 50.02, it's in the money, and holders can choose either way.
wrong.Buy 100 shares in case of assignment: If the assignment never comes, you're long 100 shares over the weekend. That's the other surprise.
wrong.Wait and see the after-hours price: Expiring options stop trading at or soon after the close, but holders have until 5:30 p.m. ET to decide. Waiting leaves you stuck.

questions.story: You're short the 50 puts and long the 55 puts, same expiry. Friday's close is 56, so both are out of the money. Minutes after the bell, news drops it to 40.
questions.q: What's your move right now?
choices: Let the broker exercise them for you
questions.why: Exercise your 55 puts. Your 50 puts can be assigned on the news. Your 55s finished out of the money at the close, so they won't be exercised unless you ask.
questions.lesson_line: After-hours news can flip an expiring spread. Know your broker's cut-off, and be ready to exercise the long leg yourself.

wrong.Nothing, both expired worthless: Holders can still exercise the 50 puts after the bell. You could be assigned with no 55s working.
wrong.Sell the 55 puts on Monday: By Monday the 55 puts have expired, and an expired option is worthless.
wrong.Let the broker exercise them for you: Automatic exercise goes off the closing price, and at 56 your 55 puts were out of the money. You have to ask.

questions.story: It's 3:45 p.m. ET on expiry Friday. You own one 50 call, and the stock is at 50.03. You don't want 100 shares over the weekend.
questions.q: What's your move?
choices: Sell it, or file a do-not-exercise
Nothing: your broker will ask first
Exercise it now to cash the 3 cents
questions.answer: Sell it, or file a do-not-exercise
questions.why: Sell it, or file a do-not-exercise. In the money by a penny or more, it's exercised unless you say otherwise, and you'd own 100 shares at 50.
questions.lesson_line: On expiry day, decide for yourself. Stay silent on an in-the-money call and you own the shares.

wrong.Nothing: 3 cents won't trigger exercise: The automatic threshold is $0.01. If it closes at 50.03, the call is in the money and gets exercised.
wrong.Nothing: your broker will ask first: Don't count on a call. Automatic exercise runs unless you give contrary instructions.
wrong.Exercise it now to cash the 3 cents: Exercising doesn't pay out cash. It buys 100 shares at 50, the thing you don't want.

questions.q: You hold a standard monthly SPX call, the AM-settled kind. When is your last chance to sell it?
questions.why: The trading day before expiry, usually Thursday. AM-settled SPX stops trading then and settles on Friday's opening prices. If you hold, those opening prices set your cash.
questions.lesson_line: With AM-settled index options, the day before expiry is your last exit. Overnight news lands on your settlement.

wrong.Friday's open, before settlement: AM-settled SPX doesn't trade on expiry day. Friday's opening prices only set the settlement value.
wrong.Monday, once it's cash-settled: After expiry there's nothing left to sell. It settles straight to cash.
wrong.Friday's 4 p.m. ET close: That's SPXW, the PM-settled version, which trades until 4:00 pm ET on expiry day.

conflicts: How many options are exercised: OIC's FAQ says historically 6% (72% closed out, 22% expire worthless); FINRA's assignment insight says 'about 7%'. q02 keys only that most contracts are NOT exercised and shows both numbers with their publishers.

Last trading day for European-style index options: OIC's FAQ says Thursday before expiration is 'typically' the last trading day for them, but Cboe's own spec says PM-settled SPXW trades until 4:00 pm ET on expiry day. q22 asks only about the AM-settled standard SPX (Cboe spec + the disclosure document) and does not use the OIC generalisation.

Exercise cut-off clock: OIC's FAQ and Schwab give 4:30 p.m. CT; FINRA Rule 2360 says 5:30 p.m. ET. Same moment; the file uses FINRA's ET wording and says 'under FINRA's rule as of November 2026'. FINRA's rule covers stock and ETF options, not index options (f39), so q10 asks about a stock option.

Automatic-exercise threshold: OCC uses $0.01 for clearing-member positions, and OIC adds 'your firm may have a different threshold'. q05 names OCC as the one exercising; its why says your broker may use its own threshold.
FINRA's assignment insight describes SPX options as 'tied to S&P 500 futures contracts'; Cboe describes them as options on the S&P 500 index. Not used anywhere in this file.

Fidelity's covered-call example says the call owner 'will likely exercise ... on the day before the ex-dividend date' and the writer 'will be assigned on the ex-dividend date'. Both fit the disclosure document (exercise before the ex-date, assignment before the next open); q13 and q16 say 'exercised the day before the ex-date' and 'assigned tonight'.

When expiring options stop trading: Schwab's expiration article (April 2026) says expiring PM-settled options typically stop at 3 p.m. CT (some ETF options 3:15 p.m. CT). Cboe's extended-hours FAQ (last updated November 2, 2026) says expiring options in its select extended-hours stock classes trade until 4:15 p.m. ET in a Curb session on expiry day, while OCC still sets in or out of the money from the 4:00 p.m. ET close (f91, f92). The file never says an expiring option can't trade after 4:00 p.m. ET; q19 says they stop 'at or soon after the close'.
